title: Predischarge counseling: explore the patient's concerns (open-ended)
vignette: A 73-year-old woman with congestive heart failure is being prepared for discharge from the hospital. The patient has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and has been admitted to the hospital twice in the past 60 days. Medical history is notable for ischemic heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and hypertension. Vital signs are normal. Pulmonary examination shows normal respiratory effort and no crackles, and there is no peripheral edema. The patient asks to stay in the hospital for a few additional days and says, "I feel fine right now, but I am worried that if I go home, I might end up back in the hospital again." Which of the following is the most appropriate response to this patient's request?

clues.text: admitted to the hospital twice in the past 60 days
clues.note: Frequent readmissions signal barriers to self-management at home that predischarge counseling should uncover.

clues.text: I feel fine right now, but I am worried that if I go home, I might end up back in the hospital again
clues.note: The patient voices a specific fear about home; the best response EXPLORES her understanding/concerns rather than jumping to solutions.

whatMatters: Effective predischarge counseling begins by EXPLORING the patient's own understanding and concerns about what could go wrong at home (an open-ended, patient-centered question). This surfaces the real, modifiable barriers to readmission before offering solutions. Answer D ('What do you think are some reasons why your heart failure might be worse at home?').
strategy: Choose the open-ended, patient-centered response that elicits her concerns and health literacy BEFORE prescribing a fix. Reject responses that jump to a specific solution prematurely (enlisting family, salt/diet, nursing home) or that dismiss her worry (she's stabilized, why stay) - these skip the crucial step of understanding her perspective.

options.text: "Managing heart failure at home can be difficult. What family members are nearby who can help?"
"Since you are worried about going home, would you like to go to a nursing home until you feel more confident?"
"Some people with heart failure have problems due to too much salt intake. Can you tell me about your diet?"
"What do you think are some reasons why your heart failure might be worse at home?"
"Your condition has now stabilized. What benefit are you hoping to gain from a continued stay?"

eliminations.label: Jump to family support - premature solution (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: enlisting family before understanding the problem. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: family help can be valuable, but it is premature to prescribe a solution before eliciting the patient's own understanding of what leads to readmission. ✅ Correct if: after her concerns are explored and support is identified as the gap.

eliminations.label: Offer a nursing home - inappropriate/premature
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: suggesting a skilled facility. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: postacute heart-failure care usually involves oral meds manageable at home; a nursing home isn't indicated and skips understanding her concerns. ✅ Correct if: she needs technically advanced skilled care (e.g., IV antibiotics, wound care).

eliminations.label: Focus on salt/diet - narrows prematurely
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: assuming dietary indiscretion is the cause. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it presumes one factor before assessing the patient's overall understanding; explore first, then target specifics like diet. ✅ Correct if: after her account points to dietary sodium as the issue.

eliminations.label: Emphasize she's stabilized - dismissive of her worry
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: highlighting clinical stability and questioning the benefit of staying. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it can feel dismissive; the goal is to address her fear of readmission by exploring home factors, not to argue against staying. ✅ Correct if: never - engage her concern, don't dismiss it.

reasoning: Patient with recurrent readmissions voices a fear about managing at home
Best predischarge counseling explores the patient's understanding/concerns first (open-ended)
This surfaces the real, modifiable barriers to readmission before offering solutions
-> 'What do you think are some reasons why your heart failure might be worse at home?'; answer D
mechanism: Heart failure carries a high 30-day readmission rate, driven by variable, often modifiable factors: premature discharge, inadequate outpatient follow-up, poor social support, dietary indiscretion (excess sodium/fluid), and medication errors or misunderstanding. Effective predischarge counseling is PATIENT-CENTERED: it begins by exploring the patient's LEVEL OF UNDERSTANDING and HEALTH LITERACY and giving her the chance to voice her specific questions and concerns about factors at home that could lead to readmission. An OPEN-ENDED question ('What do you think are some reasons your heart failure might be worse at home?') elicits her perspective, reveals knowledge gaps and barriers, and allows tailored teaching (medication purpose/dosing, symptom monitoring, sodium/fluid limits, follow-up plans) - ideally reinforced by a multidisciplinary team and follow-up phone calls/telemonitoring. Responses that jump to a single solution (family help, diet, nursing home) or dismiss her worry skip this essential assessment step; hence the open-ended exploratory question is most appropriate.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Family support, diet, and nursing home are premature solutions; 'you're stabilized' dismisses her worry - all skip exploring her perspective.
